title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Azoles. Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole inhibit ergosterol synthesis; many interactions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Why combine. Better diffusion, broader spectrum, lower doses (tolerance), prevent resistance.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Echinocandins. Caspofungin, anidulafungin, micafungin inhibit β-D-glucan synthesis in the cell wall; IV only.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Flucytosine. Blocks DNA/RNA synthesis; always used in combination (e.g. cryptococcosis); marrow toxicity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Polyenes. Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane; fungicidal; broad spectrum; nephrotoxic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Main toxicities. Amphotericin: infusion reactions, renal failure, low K and Mg; azoles: hepatitis, QT; 5-FC: marrow, gut, liver.
Topical: limited, non-recurrent superficial mycoses. Systemic: invasive (visceral/septicaemic) and extensive, recurrent or chronic superficial mycoses.
Polyenes (bind ergosterol), azoles (block ergosterol synthesis), echinocandins (block β-D-glucan), 5-flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis).
Potentiate and improve diffusion, broaden spectrum, lower doses (better tolerance), prevent resistant mutants.
Deoxycholate, liposomal, lipid complex; IV only; poor CSF (lipid better); infusion reactions, renal failure, ↓K, ↓Mg, anaemia.
Candida (not krusei), Cryptococcus; fungistatic; always combined; 90% oral bioavailability; good CSF; GI, liver, marrow toxicity.
Fluconazole: Candida, Cryptococcus (no Aspergillus, no C. krusei). Itra/vori/posa/isavu: Aspergillus. Posa/isavu: Mucorales.
Hepatotoxicity, rash, QT prolongation (isavuconazole shortens); itraconazole: ↓K, hypertension, oedema; voriconazole: hallucinations, photosensitivity, skin cancer.
Aspergillus and Candida (incl. krusei, glabrata); no Cryptococcus or Mucorales; IV only; poor CSF/urine; few interactions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-CMV. Ganciclovir IV and valganciclovir oral (myelotoxic), foscarnet (nephrotoxic), cidofovir (spaced dosing, with probenecid).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-influenza. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir), baloxavir; amantadine no longer used.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HBV. Tenofovir first line; entecavir; second line telbivudine, adefovir; lamivudine (resistance); interferons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HCV. Protease (-previr), NS5A (-asvir) and polymerase (-buvir) inhibitors; sofosbuvir + daclatasvir/velpatasvir in Morocco.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antiretrovirals. NRTIs (chain termination), NNRTIs (allosteric), protease, integrase and entry inhibitors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HSV/VZV. Acyclovir (best on HSV), valaciclovir (3× acyclovir levels, very active on VZV), famciclovir (prodrug of penciclovir).
HHV-1 HSV-1, HHV-2 HSV-2, HHV-3 VZV, HHV-4 EBV, HHV-5 CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8 KSHV.
Acyclovir: DNA polymerase inhibitor, HSV ≫ VZV, adjust to renal function. Valaciclovir: 3× levels, strong on VZV. Famciclovir: prodrug of penciclovir, HSV and VZV.
Ganciclovir IV/valganciclovir oral: myelotoxic. Foscarnet: nephrotoxic, Ca/K disturbances, genital ulcers. Cidofovir: t½ 65 h, spaced dosing, probenecid, renal failure, uveitis.
First: tenofovir (disoproxil, alafenamide), entecavir. Second: telbivudine, adefovir. Older: lamivudine (resistance). Interferons: pegylated weekly SC for 12 months.
-previr: NS3/4A protease; -asvir: NS5A; -buvir: NS5B polymerase (sofosbuvir nucleoside, dasabuvir non-nucleoside).
NRTI: nucleoside analogue, catalytic site, chain termination, competitive, higher barrier. NNRTI: non-nucleoside, allosteric site, non-competitive, low barrier.
NRTI (tenofovir, lamivudine), NNRTI (efavirenz), protease inhibitors (darunavir, atazanavir), integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir), entry inhibitors (maraviroc, enfuvirtide).
Neuraminidase inhibitors: oseltamivir (oral, < 48 h), zanamivir (inhaled), peramivir (IV); baloxavir (RNA transcription); amantadine/rimantadine obsolete.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Concentration-dependent killing. Efficacy depends on the peak/MIC: one high daily dose; post-antibiotic effect.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: The germ. Empiric choice from the usual bacteria at that site and place of acquisition, then adapt to the isolated germ and its susceptibility.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Host conditions. Extremes of age, pregnancy and lactation, renal or hepatic dysfunction, allergy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Resistance. Usually susceptible (group A streptococcus), increasing (H. influenzae, pneumococcus), multiresistant (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Site of infection. Tissue diffusion, renal or biliary elimination, intracellular diffusion for Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Time-dependent killing. Efficacy depends on time above MIC: divide doses or infuse continuously.

title: What are antibiotics and their goals?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What are antibiotics and their goals?
body.back: Antimicrobials (natural or synthetic) that kill or stop bacteria; used for bacterial infections and prophylaxis; goals: efficacy, tolerance, minimum cost.
Cell wall synthesis inhibition, membrane disruption, protein synthesis inhibition (ribosome), nucleic acid synthesis inhibition, folate synthesis inhibition.
Time: T > MIC; β-lactams, vancomycin, macrolides; divide doses/infuse. Concentration: peak/MIC; aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones; once daily, post-antibiotic effect.

title: Four criteria to choose an antibiotic?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: Four criteria to choose an antibiotic?
body.back: The germ, the site of infection, resistance, the host (age, pregnancy, organ function, allergy).
Usually susceptible: group A streptococcus. Increasing: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae. Multiresistant: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter.
Cyclins, aminoglycosides, quinolones, high-dose metronidazole; penicillins and cephalosporins are safe.
Synergy (septicaemia, endocarditis, listeriosis, nosocomial, brucellosis), critically ill empiric therapy, polymicrobial infections, preventing resistance (TB, staph with quinolone).

title: How do you assess treatment response?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: How do you assess treatment response?
body.back: Clinical (fever, tachycardia, confusion, local signs, no relapse), labs (WBC, CRP, negative cultures), imaging, side effects.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antibiotics. Shorten symptoms and shedding: doxycycline first line; azithromycin, ciprofloxacin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Typical cholera. Profuse watery rice-water stools without fever, vomiting, cramps.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rehydration. The cornerstone: oral rehydration salts, IV Ringer lactate if severe.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Complications. Severe dehydration, hypovolaemic shock and acute renal failure if untreated.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cholera toxin. The main virulence factor: blocks normal reabsorption and drives secretory diarrhoea.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transmission. Faecal-oral, through contaminated water or food; poor hygiene, disasters, wars.
Gram-negative, facultatively aerobic, comma-shaped rod with a polar flagellum; produces cholera toxin.
Cholera toxin disrupts normal fluid reabsorption → massive secretory diarrhoea up to 15 L/day → dehydration.
Incubation hours-5 days; profuse rice-water stools, afebrile, vomiting, cramps, severe dehydration; risk of shock and renal failure.
Clinical picture in an epidemic; stool culture on TCBS; rapid antigen test (less sensitive); PCR.
Rehydration (ORS; IV Ringer lactate if severe); doxycycline single dose; azithromycin (children) or ciprofloxacin.
Safe water, sanitation, hand washing; oral inactivated vaccines (Dukoral, Shanchol, Euvichol); surveillance and rapid response.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bucco-oesophageal candidiasis. Dysphagia, retrosternal pain, whitish coating; endoscopy, fluconazole, HIV test.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CMV infection. CD4 < 50; retinitis with exudates and haemorrhagic necrosis; also colitis, oesophagitis, encephalitis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cryptosporidiosis. Intestinal (acute or chronic diarrhoea) or biliary (sclerosing cholangitis); stool exam, biopsy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Kaposi sarcoma. Purple-brown macules, nodules, plaques; mucosal and visceral forms; biopsy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Other cancers. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (EBV), cervical cancer (HPV); HIV promotes but does not directly cause cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tuberculosis. The most frequent OI at all stages; HIV raises TB risk and TB raises HIV replication.

title: Oesophageal candidiasis in HIV: signs and management?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: Oesophageal candidiasis in HIV: signs and management?
body.back: Dysphagia, retrosternal pain, whitish oropharyngeal coating; upper GI endoscopy; fluconazole; HIV screening.
HIV destroys Th1 cells and reduces IFN-γ (↑ TB risk); TB stimulates TNF, IL-1, IL-6 (↑ HIV replication).
More extensive and severe forms, resistant bacilli, more drug side effects.
CD4 < 50; retinitis (exudates, haemorrhagic necrosis, blindness risk); colitis, oesophagitis, cholangitis, encephalitis, myelitis, pneumonia.
Intestinal (diarrhoea, pain) or biliary (sclerosing cholangitis); stool parasitology, colonoscopic biopsy, ultrasound.
HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma. EBV: non-Hodgkin lymphoma. HPV: cervical cancer.
Purple-brown macules, pigmented papulo-nodules, angiomatoid nodules, infiltrated/verrucous/ulcerated plaques; limb lymphoedema; mucosal and visceral forms; biopsy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antiretroviral therapy. At least three drugs for life: 2 NRTIs + an NNRTI, a protease inhibitor or an integrase inhibitor.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Early infection. Primary infection then a long asymptomatic phase (CDC category A).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Below 200 CD4/mm³. AIDS: Pneumocystis pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Moderate immunosuppression. Minor infections, TB, candidiasis, shingles, Kaposi sarcoma (category B).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prevention. Abstinence, fidelity, condoms, PrEP (TDF/FTC), post-exposure prophylaxis, prevention of mother-to-child transmission.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Below 100 CD4/mm³. Cryptococcal meningitis, CMV retinitis, MAC, lymphomas.

title: Why is HIV now a chronic disease?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: Why is HIV now a chronic disease?
body.back: With ART it progresses slowly and life expectancy approaches normal, but there is no cure or vaccine and treatment is lifelong.
HIV-1 (worldwide), HIV-2 (West Africa). CD4+ T lymphocytes (90% of infected cells) and brain glial cells.
Prevalence ~0.08%; concentrated in key populations (PWID, sex workers, MSM); mainly heterosexual transmission; 25-44 years most affected.
HIV-negative, over 18, HBV-vaccinated, at regular risk; TDF/FTC 1 tablet daily until 2 days after last exposure; no protection against other STIs or HCV.
Triple therapy ideally within 4 h, no later than 48-72 h, for 4 weeks.
Maternal ARVs, no breastfeeding, delivery mode by viral load, newborn ARV syrup for 1 month: risk < 1% (vs 25-40%).
Screen with 4th-generation ELISA (Ab + p24) or rapid test; confirm with plasma viral load; Western blot only for discordance.
Early: TB, candidiasis, Kaposi. < 200: Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis. < 100: cryptococcosis, CMV, MAC, lymphoma.
Undetectable viral load, CD4 recovery, better quality of life, less transmission; ≥ 3 drugs, uninterrupted, lifelong, strict adherence, check interactions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anicteric form. Sudden flu-like illness, self-limited, rarely fatal; may relapse with aseptic meningitis (immune stage).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis. Dark-field microscopy and culture; PCR (blood, from day 1); ELISA IgM (day 8); MAT, the reference (day 10); two sera 15 days apart.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Portal of entry. Cuts, abraded skin, mucous membranes or conjunctivae in contact with contaminated water or soil.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Icteric form. Severe: fever, jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage, respiratory distress; heart, CNS and muscle involvement.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reservoir. Rodents (rats, mice) and domestic animals shed leptospires in urine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Treatment. Penicillin G or amoxicillin 10 days, ceftriaxone 7-10 days or doxycycline 7 days, plus supportive care and dialysis.
A zoonosis due to spirochetes of the genus Leptospira; L. interrogans is pathogenic (230 serovars, 23 serogroups); L. biflexa is saprophytic.
Contact with animal urine, contaminated water or soil (public baths) or infected tissue, through cuts, abraded skin, mucosa or conjunctivae.
Slaughterhouse workers, miners, sewer workers, garbage collectors; often an occupational disease.
Anicteric: sudden flu-like, self-limited, possible immune stage with aseptic meningitis. Icteric: fever, jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage, respiratory distress.
Dark-field microscopy, culture; PCR from D1; ELISA IgM from D8 (> 1/400); MAT reference from D10 (> 1/100); two sera 15 days apart.
Penicillin G or amoxicillin 10 days, ceftriaxone 7-10 days, or doxycycline 7 days; fluids, transfusion, dialysis, resuscitation.
Rodent control (public baths), bathing hygiene, gloves/boots/glasses and wound protection, vaccination for exposed workers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bloody CSF. Three-tube test: clearing and clots suggest a traumatic tap; no clearing suggests intracranial bleeding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clear lymphocytic, low glucose. Tuberculous (protein > 1 g/L), Listeria, or partially treated ('decapitated') bacterial meningitis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Viral meningitis. Under 100 lymphocytes, normal glucose.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lumbar puncture. Performed after a neurological exam; contraindicated with skin sepsis, coagulopathy, raised ICP or a mass; never delays antibiotics.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Purulent meningitis. ≥ 1,000 cells/mm³, neutrophils, high protein, low glucose: meningococcus or pneumococcus.
Inflammation of the meninges: bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic or non-infectious; a medical emergency.
Adults: meningococcus, pneumococcus, TB. Newborns: GBS, E. coli, Listeria, TB. Older children: meningococcus, pneumococcus, Hib, TB.
Headache, vomiting, nuchal rigidity, photophobia (+ fever); Kernig and Brudzinski signs; severity: purpura, deficit, coma, shock.
Local skin sepsis, bleeding coagulopathy, raised ICP, suspected intracranial mass (fundus and CT check herniation risk).
Normal < 3 cells, protein < 0.4, ratio 0.5. Bacterial: ≥ 1,000 PMN, glucose ↓. TB/Listeria: lymphocytes, protein ↑, glucose ↓. Viral: < 100 lymphocytes, glucose normal.
Epidemic potential; phone notification; droplet spread; sudden onset; purpura (fulminans = severe).
Progressive onset, weight loss, mental changes, oculomotor palsy; clear lymphocytic CSF, protein > 1 g/L, low glucose; hyponatraemia.
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/d or cefotaxime 200-300 mg/kg/d IV (7 d meningo, 10-14 d pneumo); TB: 2RHZE/7RH + steroids; Listeria: amoxicillin + gentamicin 2-3 weeks.
Rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 2 days (or spiramycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin) + vaccination.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Definition. Temperature above 38.3 °C on repeated measurements for at least 3 weeks without a cause after examination and routine tests.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Infectious causes. TB (first cause in developing countries), typhoid, endocarditis, deep abscesses, brucellosis, malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, HIV, CMV, EBV, fungi.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammatory diseases. 25-30%: Horton disease (elderly), Still disease (young adult), lupus, IBD, vasculitides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Miscellaneous. Thromboembolism, deep haematoma, drug fever, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, thermal dysregulation, factitious fever.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neoplasms. Lymphomas, leukaemias; kidney, liver, digestive, lung and other solid tumours.
Temperature > 38.3 °C, repeated, for 3 weeks, without an obvious cause after clinical examination and routine tests.
Common; blind antibiotics cause resistance and delay diagnosis; many causes; ~25% undiagnosed.
Infections, systemic inflammatory diseases, neoplasms, miscellaneous (+ undiagnosed).
TB (first in developing countries), typhoid, endocarditis, deep abscesses, focal infections, malaria, leishmaniasis, amoebiasis, HIV, CMV, EBV, fungi.
Thromboembolism, deep haematoma, drug fever, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, thermal dysregulation, factitious fever.
Vet/dairy: brucellosis; sewer/rat urine/fresh water: leptospirosis; butcher: toxoplasmosis; dog ticks: rickettsiosis; raw fish/plants: distomatosis.
Neutropenic, splenectomised, valvular disease, cancer, cirrhosis, immunocompromised, HIV with CD4 < 200, prosthesis, poorly tolerated fever.
CBC, ≥ 3 blood cultures, urine, CRP/ESR/fibrinogen/EPP, biochemistry, CXR, TB tests, serologies, thick smear, sinus/dental X-rays, ultrasound, ANA, TSH.
Special cultures, LP, echocardiography, vascular ultrasound, CT, endoscopies, bronchoscopy, bone scintigraphy, brain MRI, biopsies (temporal artery).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exposure. Bites, scratches or licks on broken skin or mucosa; in Morocco the dog is the animal in 89% of cases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: State phase. Furious rabies (hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, dysautonomia, clear consciousness) or paralytic rabies; death in 3-6 days.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Incubation. Silent, usually 20-60 days; shorter in children and with bites near the head.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neural spread. The virus migrates along peripheral nerves to the spinal ganglion and CNS, then out to the salivary glands.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Post-exposure prophylaxis. Immediate wound cleaning, severity assessment at an anti-rabies centre, vaccination and specific immunoglobulins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prodrome. Tingling or itching at the bite in 50-80%, anxiety, insomnia, fever, digestive signs.
A viral zoonosis of domestic and wild animals causing always-fatal encephalomyelitis; treatment is only preventive.
Saliva via bites, scratches, licks on broken skin or mucosa; human-to-human by corneal transplant.
< 20 years (54%), male (73%), rural (79%); dog in 89%, cat in 5%.
Virus climbs peripheral nerves to spinal ganglion and CNS (rhinencephalon), replicates, then spreads along nerves to salivary glands.
Usually 20-60 days (15 d-1 yr), shorter in children and near-head bites; allows vaccination before symptoms.
Furious: agitation, hallucinations, hydrophobia, aerophobia, dysautonomia, clear consciousness. Paralytic: ascending flaccid paralysis, bulbar signs. Death in 3-6 days.
Clean the wound at once; assess severity at an anti-rabies centre; vaccination ± specific immunoglobulins; observe the biting animal.
Health education; vaccinate domestic animals; remove stray dogs and cats; control pet imports.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inoculation. Painless bite (anaesthetic saliva) lasting at least 20 hours, in armpits, groin, genital area.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Complicated forms. Purpura, jaundice, confusion, seizures, coma, renal failure, thrombosis, bleeding, arrhythmias; risk: age > 60, diabetes, alcohol, G6PD deficiency.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis. Clinical first; immunofluorescence IgG/IgM (≥ 1/128 or rising titres 15 days apart); PCR or culture from blood or skin biopsy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Treatment. Doxycycline 200 mg/day for 5-7 days (or until 2 days after fever); josamycin for newborns, children and pregnant women.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vector and reservoir. The brown dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus; contact with dogs matters; summer (July-September in Morocco).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical triad. Sudden fever to 39.5 °C, maculopapular rash starting on the trunk, and the black eschar (tache noire) in 80%.

title: Agent, vector and reservoir of Mediterranean spotted fever?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: Agent, vector and reservoir of Mediterranean spotted fever?
body.back: Rickettsia conorii; the dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus is both vector and reservoir.
Mediterranean, summer (July-September), linked to contact with dogs.
Sudden fever (~39.5 °C) with flu-like illness, maculopapular rash starting on the trunk, black inoculation eschar (80%).
6-7%: purpura, jaundice, confusion, seizures, coma, renal failure, thrombosis, bleeding, arrhythmia; age > 60, diabetes, alcohol, smoking, immunosuppression, G6PD deficiency.
IFA IgG/IgM ≥ 1/128 or rising titres (15 days), Western blot; PCR/culture from blood or eschar biopsy; ↓ platelets, Na, Ca; ↑ transaminases.
Doxycycline 200 mg/day 5-7 days; josamycin for children and pregnancy; repellents, remove ticks < 20 h, control stray dogs, anti-tick collars.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Definition. At least two grouped cases with similar, usually digestive, symptoms linked to the same food; mandatory reporting.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Febrile, invasive. Salmonella (12-24 h; eggs, poultry, meat, seafood), Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia (48-72 h).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Management. Rehydration first; antibiotics (fluoroquinolone, azithromycin, cotrimoxazole) only for specific indications; investigation of the source.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clostridium perfringens. Isolated diarrhoea without fever; dishes made the day before, poor refrigeration, collective catering.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:infectious

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Short incubation, afebrile. Preformed toxin: Staphylococcus aureus (2-4 h; vomiting, pain; dairy and dishes made the day before), Bacillus cereus.
At least two grouped cases with similar, usually digestive, symptoms linked to the same food source; notifiable.
Preformed toxins: S. aureus (2-4 h; vomiting, pain; dairy, dishes made the day before), Bacillus cereus; C. perfringens (isolated afebrile diarrhoea).
Salmonella (12-24 h; eggs, poultry, meat, seafood); Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia (48-72 h).
Rehydration, antipyretics, early refeeding, avoid stimulating foods, antisecretory agents; no transit slowers in invasive diarrhoea.
Symptoms > 48-72 h, suspected salmonellosis, bacterial dysentery, cholera, or risk factors (infant, elderly, immunocompromised, valve disease); fluoroquinolone, azithromycin, cotrimoxazole.
Mandatory reporting, epidemiological investigation, identify and remove food, find faulty procedures, test kitchen staff.
Hand washing, clean utensils and surfaces, no cooked-raw contact, < 2 h out of fridge, fridge < 4.5 °C, cook eggs and meat thoroughly.
